title: UOHF Definition 2.0: Unified Ontology of Human Function
abstract: This publication presents UOHF Definition 2.0, a task-centered semantic and computational architecture for representing, assessing, and governing human function in real-world contexts. The central problem addressed by Definition 2.0 is that medical records, rehabilitation assessments, exercise data, movement observations, task performance, symptoms, measurements, interventions, and follow-up information may all concern the same person, yet they do not automatically form one coherent and continuously updated human-function object. Different disciplines often describe different fragments of the person, use different judgment units, and apply different professional languages. As a result, information may accumulate without producing a unified account of what the person is being asked to do, what the body must organize, what actually occurs, what costs arise, where the boundary lies, and what changes after action or exposure. UOHF Definition 2.0 establishes a common operational center: Human function is understood through the relationship between real-world tasks, the functional capacities required by those tasks, the way the body is actually engaged, the resulting performance and cost, and the boundaries within which that engagement remains sustainable and safe. Definition 2.0 formalizes a task-centered reasoning chain: Safety Boundary → Task and Context → Task Demand → Required Engagement → Actual Engagement → Manifestation and Measurement → Cost and Boundary → Limiting-Factor Hypotheses → Evidence Convergence → Primary Problem → State → Governed Action → Execution → Actual Change → Feedback → Reassessment → Versioned Write-back Within this architecture, a Task is not treated as identical to the demands generated by that task. A task such as walking, climbing stairs, lifting, sitting, working, exercising, or caring for another person occurs under specific contextual conditions. Speed, duration, load, environment, complexity, role, consequence, and recovery requirements may change the demands placed on the body even when the named task remains the same. Definition 2.0 therefore distinguishes the task itself from the task conditions and from the functional organization required to meet those conditions. It also distinguishes: the functional capacity that may exist in the person; the engagement required by the task; the engagement that required by the task; the engagement that actually occurs; the observable manifestation of that engagement; the measurement or report used as evidence; the inference formed from that evidence; the state representation recorded by the system. These distinctions prevent performance, measurement, diagnosis, capacity, bodily process, and human-function state from being collapsed into a single label. A person may complete a task while relying on compensation, elevated effort, pain, instability, excessive physiological cost, delayed recovery, reduced reserve, or exposure to unacceptable risk. Task completion alone therefore does not establish normal human function. Definition 2.0 evaluates whether the task goal is achieved, whether the organization is sufficiently stable, and whether the associated cost remains controllable within the relevant safety and sustainability boundaries. The framework uses four person-level, task-centered state classes: Normal Functional State Compensatory Functional State Boundary-Critical Functional State Functional Incapacity State These states are not medical diagnoses, permanent identities, or universal classifications of organs, tissues, cells, or molecular processes. They are evidence-bounded representations of how the body functions under specified tasks and conditions. Definition 2.0 also establishes a strict separation between the reality of the person, the evidence used to understand that reality, and the actions taken to influence it. The reality layer includes the person, task, context, functional capacity, actual engagement, bodily response, cost, boundary, reserve, state, time, and actual change. The epistemic layer includes observation, questioning, measurement, assessment, evidence, uncertainty, inference, and professional judgment. The application layer includes medical treatment, rehabilitation, exercise, training, environmental modification, assist, assessment, evidence, uncertainty, inference, and professional judgment. Theive technology, education, and other governed actions. An assessment tool does not define human function. A measurement does not equal the bodily reality it is intended to represent. An intervention does not belong to the human-function state itself. These elements must be connected but not conflated. Definition 2.0 further separates four connected system components: UOHF, the governed ontology and semantic-rule layer; the Human Function Engine, the bounded runtime inference and write-back layer; the Individual Human Function Model, the person-specific longitudinal state memory; the Human Function World Model, the future temporal and action-conditioned modeling layer. The publication emphasizes auditable reasoning, explicit evidence boundaries, safety constraints, authority control, version governance, reassessment, and longitudinal write-back. It does not support unrestricted black-box conclusions or autonomous diagnosis and treatment. UOHF Definition 2.0 is a conceptual and operational framework rather than a completed international standard. It does not claim that all human functions, all task-demand relations, all physiological mechanisms, all professional mappings, or a fully axiomatized machine-readable ontology have already been completed. Its principal contribution is the establishment of a task-centered, evidence-bounded, safety-constrained, and auditable architecture through which human-function information can be organized around the same person and continuously updated across assessment, action, execution, feedback, and reassessment.

title: UOHF Definition 2.1: Unified Ontology of Human Function
abstract: This publication presents UOHF Definition 2.1, the current authoritative conceptual definition and ontology architecture of the Unified Ontology of Human Function. Definition 2.1 retains the task-centered operational achievements of Definition 2.0 while correcting and expanding the scope of human function beyond real-world tasks alone. The human body is continuously engaged not only by external behavior, environment, and life tasks, but also by internal requirements for physiological maintenance, regulation, development, defense, adaptation, repair, and recovery. The formal definition is: Human function is the body's capacity to be appropriately engaged to meet internal and external demands. The corresponding Chinese philosophical definition is: 人体功能=身体被正常调用的能力。 In this definition, Demand includes ongoing internal requirements for physiological maintenance, regulation, development, defense, adaptation, repair, and recovery, as well as external behavioral, environmental, and real-world task demands. Definition 2.1 therefore establishes Demand, rather than Task alone, as the broader condition under which human function must be understood. A Task remains an important type of external activity or context, but a task is not identical to the demand it generates. The same task may produce different demands depending on load, duration, speed, environment, complexity, consequence, role, individual condition, and time. Internal physiological demands may also arise without any visible external task, including during sleep, rest, infection, injury, growth, adaptation, repair, or recovery. Definition 2.1 distinguishes: Demand, the internal or external requirement condition; Demand Specification, the versioned informational description of that demand; Task, a goal-directed activity or activity context; Task Demand, the external requirements generated by a task under specified conditions; Task Demand Specification, the versioned representation of those requirements; Engagement Requirement, what must be organized to meet the demand; Required Engagement Process Type, the expected process type capable of satisfying that requirement; Actual Engagement Process, the organization that actually occurs in the person; Actual Engagement Inference, the evidence-bounded conclusion about that process; Actual Engagement Representation, the versioned record of the inference. These entities are related but are not identical. Definition 2.1 generalizes Functional Engagement from a task-centered concept to a demand-centered concept. Functional engagement is the organization through which the body responds to an internal or external demand. Depending on scale and context, it may include molecular and cellular processes, tissue and organ processes, interactions among organ systems, structural support, functional capacities, sensory feedback, motor control, energy supply, metabolic regulation, protection, defense, adaptation, repair, recovery, cognition, behavior, and interaction with environmental conditions. Functional engagement does not mean conscious command, voluntary participation, patient engagement, service engagement, isolated neural activation, or one muscle contraction. It refers to the organized operation of the relevant human functions under a specified demand. The formal human-function definition includes the phrase appropriately engaged because the required functions must not merely operate. They must operate in a manner appropriate to the current demand, the person’s conditions, the available evidence, and the relevant safety and sustainability boundaries. At a general level, appropriate engagement requires that: the demand is sufficiently met; the organization remains sufficiently stable and adaptable; the associated cost and regulatory burden remain within sustainable boundaries appropriate to the context, time, and demand. Safety boundaries remain an independent constraint layer. Definition 2.1 also distinguishes the reality of human function from the evidence and representations used to describe it. Human function is not identical to human-function state.Demand is not identical to Demand Specification.Actual Engagement Process is not identical to Actual Engagement Inference.Actual response is not identical to manifestation or measurement result.Immediate cost is not identical to accumulated burden.Boundary is not identical to reserve.State is not identical to StateActual Inference or State Representation.Actual change is not identical to feedback information. This reality–evidence–inference–representation separation is essential for auditable reasoning, uncertainty management, provenance, version governance, and safe artificial intelligence. Definition 2.1 organizes UOHF into four connected components: UOHF — the governed ontology and semantic-rule foundation; the Human Function Engine — the bounded inference, state-convergence, action-control, and write-back layer; the Individual Human Function Model — the person-specific longitudinal representation of human-function state; the Human Function World Model — the temporal, multiscale, and action-conditioned modeling of human-function change. The development direction can be summarized as: Governed ontology topology → Human Function Engine → Individual longitudinal model → Human Function World Model The final scope of the Human Function World Model includes molecules, cells, tissues, bodily structures, organs, organ systems, physiological processes, cross-organ interactions, clinical mechanisms, disease, functional capacities, functional engagement, behavior, tasks, life contexts, and environment. These must be connected through state, cost, boundary, time, feedback, events, and change. Definition 2.1 does not treat local biological function as synonymous with whole-person human function. Molecular, cellular, tissue, organ, and system functions form the mechanisms, foundations, or limiting conditions through which whole-person human function is realized. UOHF must connect these scales without collapsing them into one ontological level. The framework also provides a unified interpretation of medicine, rehabilitation, and exercise: functional capacity → restoration of appropriate engagement → maintenance and enhancement of human function and expansion of engagement boundaries Medicine primarily addresses functional capacities, their biological foundations, disease mechanisms, and safety boundaries. Rehabilitation primarily addresses the return of functional capacities to real-world tasks and the restoration of appropriate engagement. Exercise maintains and enhances human function and expands engagement boundaries through sustained, appropriately dosed, and progressive engagement. Psychology and nutrition enter according to the current primary limiting factor, evidence, and professional scope. These are principal objectives rather than absolute professional boundaries. The current operational implementation remains strongest in task-centered assessment, state convergence, governed action, execution feedback, reassessment, and longitudinal service workflows. Definition 2.1 does not claim that internal-demand operationalization, complete multiscale mappings, a universal physiological-state classification, full OWL axiomatization, external expert consensus, clinical outcome validation, or a molecular-to-person simulator have already been completed. UOHF Definition 2.1 is therefore both a scope correction and an architectural clarification. It preserves the practical task-centered framework of Definition 2.0 while establishing the broader ontological foundation required to represent the body as a continuously regulated whole under internal and external demands.

title: Validating predictive models on EHRs data : lessons learnt from the NCDR-IMPACT-score applied on a French cardiac catheterization cohort.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: We present a natural language processing pipeline to extract and re-compute a pre-existing score, the IMPACT-score, in a children's hospital belonging to the APHP hospitals. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Predictive variables and adverse events occurrences were extracted from the EHR of each patient. Data extraction involved rule-based and machine learning approaches depending on the format of the data. The machine learning text-classifiers were trained on active learning annotated dataset. Once the registry was automatically populated, we computed the IMPACT-score model in our patients and we performed a logistic regression analysis to find the specific odd ratio fitting our cohort and obtain the IMPACT-score-Necker. RESULTS: We extracted clinical data from 2,980 patients. When applied to our hospital cohort, the IMPACT-score-Necker achieved an AUC of 0.719 whereas the original IMPACT-score achieved an AUC of 0.642. As a reminder, the IMPACT-score achieved an AUC of 0.752 in the NCDR-IMPACT validation cohort. DISCUSSION: Local calibration of the IMPACT-score on our cohort enhanced predictive accuracy, improving the AUC from 0.642 to 0.719, and addressing differences between our population and the original NCDR-IMPACT cohort. This reinforces the need for model adaptation to local data, as patient demographic and clinical variations can significantly impact performance. Local EHR data warehouses could be leveraged for recalibration and continuous monitoring, ensuring that AI tools remain accurate, ethical, and practical for clinicians in their clinical practice. CONCLUSION: Our results underscore the need for real-world model validation, and EHRs offer a reliable source for training and validating AI models.
authors: S Quennelle; S Malekzadeh-Milani; N Garcelon; A Burgun; D Bonnet; A Neuraz

title: What physics offers for artificial intelligence? Lessons from the brain's inner time and its dynamics.
abstract: Computing can take advantage of physics-that is, 'whatever physics offers' (Jaeger et al. 2023 Nat. Commun. 14, 4911 (doi:10.1038/s41467-023-40533-1)). One of the key features physics provides is time: it describes rules and makes predictions about how activity patterns change over time, as governed by dynamics. We argue that computing can learn from physics in how it conceives time-namely, in terms of dynamics, i.e. the changing patterns of activity unfolding over time. In particular, we focus on the brain's intrinsic neural dynamics of spontaneous activity and how it 'uses' them for dynamic input processing and encoding in order to 'participate' in the world's physical time. By 'participate', we mean becoming part of the input dynamics: for instance, when listening or dancing to music, neural activity (via entrainment) and, consequently, mental activity follows the rhythm and dynamics of the music. This shapes the listener's experience, such as consciousness-the brain, and thus the subject, actively participates in music rhythms through temporal alignment (Northoff et al. 2023 Interface Focus13, 20220076 (doi:10.1098/rsfs.2022.0076)). Drawing on recent empirical evidence, we show that dynamic features such as the brain's scale-free activity and variability-which reflect an intrinsic temporal structure, or the brain's 'inner time'-are central to tracking and encoding input dynamics. Importantly, this processing is actively modulated rather than passively received, through the brain's own 'hidden dynamic repertoire'. Extending earlier discussions by Dreyfus and others, we argue that current computing devices, whether classical or natural (i.e. non-von Neumann machines), lack spontaneous activity and an inner time that can exert an active, rather than purely passive, influence on processing. As a result, they can neither actively process and encode input dynamics through their own inner time, nor 'use' or 'participate' in the dynamics of the world's physical time. Instead of 'being in time' and 'being in the world', current computing devices-and, by extension, artificial intelligence-are effectively 'locked out of time and world', meaning they are not directly connected to physical time. Unlike humans, they therefore cannot be characterized as 'being in time' or 'being in the world', which in turn prevents them from acquiring tacit or implicit knowledge, including the ability to navigate and behave flexibly within a continuously changing world. This article is part of the theme issue 'World models in natural and artificial intelligence'.
authors: Northoff G, Catal Y, Abbasi S.

title: WITHDRAWN: MedOS: AI-XR-Cobot World Model for Clinical Perception and Action
